in_text_mentions: [54]. However, in BD sudden hilar enlargement or intraparenchymal round opacities on the chest radiograph or chest CT scan can present pulmonary artery aneurysm [8, 14]. PAAs may be single (Figures 2–4) or multiple unilateral or bilateral (Figure 5). These lesions may be occluded totally or partially by thrombus (Figures 2, 4, 5). Thrombosed aneurysms cause ischemia or infarction in pulmonary parenchyma [8, 20]. In BD hemoptysis can also be misdiagnosed as pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) and this condition could be mistakenly attributed to PTE and inappropriate anticoagulation may prove fatal

in_text_mentions: giography (FA) is the gold standard imaging modality for retinal vasculature. FA is a mandatory tool for the assessment of inflammatory fundus conditions due to posterior uveitis; the leakage on FA identifies retinal vasculitis and is a crucial marker for BD uveitis activity [21]. Specific signs of inflammatory activity include increased retinal vein tortuosity, vessel wall staining and leakage from retinal vessels and from the optic disc (Figure 2 and Figure 3). Fern-like capillary leakage is the most characteristic FA finding of BD uveitis and may be present even when uveitis seems inactive.

in_text_mentions: that show homogeneous contrast filling simultaneously with the pulmonary artery. PAAs in BD predominantly affect the right lower lobar artery, followed by the right and left main pulmonary arteries (Figure 3 and Figure 4). They are multiple, usually pseudoaneurysms, with various diameters and in situ thrombosis [21]. The most frequent symptom is massive hemoptysis caused by aneurysm rupture with erosion into a bronchus [39]. Pulmonary aneurysms are classified using CTPA into six radiologic patterns: aneurysmatic wall enhancement on post-contrast CTPA; true “stable” pulmonary artery aneurysms

in_text_mentions: Considering recurrent hemoptysis, a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) was performed (Figure 2). In CTPA, aneurysmal dilation of the right interlobar descending artery containing a clot with an external diameter of 19 mm was observed. The central canal was open and extended peripherally. No abnormal intraluminal filling defect suggesting pulmonary embolism was observed in other pulmonary arterial structures. A rheumatological consultation and laboratory tests were performed; the results are shown in Table 1.

panels.rationale: Single intraoral clinical photograph from a case report of juvenile Behçet syndrome. The image clearly shows a round, punched-out aphthous ulcer with an erythematous halo on the left lateral border of the tongue, matching the caption and in-text description of an 8-mm aphthous ulcer. Recurrent oral aphthae are the hallmark manifestation of Behçet's disease, so disease attribution is strong. No annotations are present; the visible perioral/chin skin appears light-toned. Age is not stated in the caption or in-text mentions, so age_group is unknown. [raw subtype: juvenile]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial contrast CT of the thorax in a Behçet's disease patient showing a peribronchial lesion (green arrow) in the right lung interpreted as an aneurysm of the right main pulmonary artery; pulmonary artery aneurysm is a recognized vascular manifestation of Behçet's disease and the article title directly attributes the case to Behçet's disease. panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a circled intradermal test site showing a small erythematous papular reaction, captioned as a positive pathergy test (papule >2 mm at 48 h after sterile-needle prick). The pathergy reaction is a recognized minor diagnostic criterion for Behçet's disease and the article is a Behçet's disease case report, so attribution to behcet_disease is well supported; the manifestation matches the vocabulary entry behcet_disease_positive_pathergy_reaction. Skin tone is not reliably assessable due to the strong warm/yellow color cast, and no ethnicity, age, or body site is stated.
panels.attribution_text: Arkania et al. Behçet's Disease in a Patient With Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: A Case of Genital Ulceration Resembling a Sexually Transmitted Disease.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.91050. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: The patient’s pathergy test results indicating a positive reaction, as evidenced by the development of papules larger than 2 mm 48 hours following intradermal injection with a sterile needle.
in_text_mentions: A diagnostic skin test called the pathergy test evaluates a patient’s heightened inflammatory reaction to mild trauma, such as a needle prick. If a papule (small bump) or pustule (pimple) forms at the prick site within 24 to 48 hours, the test is considered positive. The hypersensitivity of this test makes it a minor diagnostic criterion for BD. The results of the pathergy test in this patient showed a positive reaction, marked by the formation of papules measuring more than 2 mm within 48 hours after intradermal injection using a sterile needle (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Low-power H&E of the patient skin punch biopsy in the Behçet's disease case; caption/in-text tie the biopsy to pan-dermal neutrophilic inflammation and acute vasculitis as the distinguishing Behçet's finding. Lower-specific supportive features are listed as proposed findings. B: Same human skin punch biopsy from the Behçet's disease case; panel B shows the edema/necrosis/blistering component of the biopsy captioned as acute vasculitis. The directly visible supportive features are proposed findings. C: High-power H&E directly shows neutrophilic vasculitis in the Behçet's disease biopsy; the in-text explicitly calls acute vasculitis with fibrinoid change the histopathological hallmark distinguishing Behçet's. D: High-power H&E shows dermal neutrophilic infiltrate with prominent leukocytoclasia, matching the vocabulary finding for neutrophilic leukocytoclastic vasculitis in Behçet's disease.

panels.rationale: Single axial chest CT from a real patient in a Behçet's disease article. The red arrow marks a hyperdense metallic coil within a right lower lobe pulmonary artery aneurysm, a recognized vascular manifestation of Behçet's disease explicitly named in the caption and in-text. A dependent right pleural effusion is also visible but is not in the allowed vocabulary, so it is listed only as a proposed finding. No ethnicity or age is stated; skin tone is not assessable on CT.
panels.attribution_text: Hansen and Dyke. Pulmonary Artery-Tracheal Fistula After Coil Implantation for Behcet's Disease.. Cureus 2020. doi:10.7759/cureus.11036. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: CT of the chest showing residual coil within the right lower lobe pulmonary artery aneurysm.
in_text_mentions: s hemoptysis resolved. He was well for an additional four years until he presented to us with recurrent severe cough and hemoptysis. Bronchoscopy again revealed metallic wire within the trachea and right lower lobe bronchus (Figures 1, 2). Chest CT revealed a large amount coil still within the PAA (Figure 3). After discussing these findings with the patient, he elected to undergo a right lower lobectomy with resection of the PAA and coil. Intra-operative bronchoscopy revealed a small fragment of residual wire within the right lower lobe bronchus, which was removed. His recovery was uneventful.

in_text_mentions: A chest CT angiography study was ordered and showed a filling defect in both the right and left segmental and subsegmental pulmonary arteries (Figure 1) and there was a right lower lobe PAA (2.5 x 2 cm) (Figure 2). Echocardiography was done and showed a right ventricular large thrombus (3 x 2.6 cm) and ejection fraction (EF) was 60%, with no valvular abnormality. The left ventricle (LV) was normal in size, with good contraction, and no left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). The right ventricle (RV) was normal in size and function, with no pericardial effusion.

in_text_mentions: Examination showed two aphthous ulcers, one on the inner upper lip and another on the posterior buccal mucosa/upper gingivobuccal sulcus adjacent to the maxillary molars (Figure 1A). The inguinal region showed grouped papulopustular lesions on a background of hyperpigmentation (Figure 1B), and scattered erythematous papules were present over the buttocks (Figure 1C). Musculoskeletal examination showed tenderness of both knees without effusion, deformity, or restriction of movement. Mild right upper quadrant tenderness and bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy were also noted. No other abno

ehçet's disease was suspected. A forearm pathergy test was positive, with a well‐demarcated erythematous papule and a central punctate lesion developing at the needle‐prick site after 24–48 h (Figure 1D). Relevant investigations are summarized in Table 1, and the clinical course is outlined in Table 2. Laboratory evaluation showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, mild leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis. Renal and liver screening tests, including bilirubin and routine electrolytes, were within normal limits on the available panel. Hemoglobin was normal at 13.7 g/dL, while MCV was 74.4

in_text_mentions: In physical examination, limited abduction of his left eye, erythema at injection sites (Figure 2A) and raised temperature of skin on the right inner thigh were manifest, together with swelling of bilateral lower limbs, particularly in the right. Negative results were reported in investigations including extractable nuclear antigen, lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin antibodies. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 55 mg/L (normal: < 5 mg/L). Considering the refractory thrombi in deep veins of lower limbs and dural sinus, genetic screening for thrombophilia which used panel-based next generation

nd confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The variant of TFPI was also identified in his father but not his mother through further work-up. Meanwhile, the patient began to exhibit two ulcers on the scrotum (Figure 2B). But no oral aphthae were found with the patient. After repeated questioning, the patient reported recurrent genital ulcerations for half a year, and resolution always occurred spontaneously. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Real patient clinical photograph of a genital ulcer on the inner left labia minora, explicitly captioned and confirmed in the text as a genital ulcer in a patient diagnosed with incomplete-type Behçet's disease with recurrent genital and oral ulcerations. [raw subtype: incomplete] b: Real patient clinical photograph of a 5 mm aphthous ulcer on the left side of the tongue, explicitly captioned and confirmed in the text as part of recurrent oral ulcerations (herpetiform) in a patient diagnosed with incomplete-type Behçet's disease. findings.evidence: Forearm showing four intradermal prick sites with pen markings; erythematous papules or pustules at 24 hours indicate a positive pathergy test

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of forearm pathergy test at 24 hours showing erythematous papules and pustules at intradermal prick sites; in-text explicitly states this reflects the hyperreactive inflammatory response characteristic of Behçet's disease and fulfills a minor ISG diagnostic criterion. B: Clinical photograph of forearm pathergy test at 48 hours confirming positive pathergy reaction with erythematous papules and pustules at prick sites; directly attributed to Behçet's disease per in-text discussion.
panels.attribution_text: Batool et al. Behçet's Disease Mimicking Drug-Induced Mucocutaneous Lesions in a Patient on Anti-tuberculous Drugs.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.96922. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Pathergy test (A) Forearm showing four intradermal prick sites with pen markings; erythematous papules or pustules at 24 hours indicate a positive pathergy test. (B) Similar findings observed at 48 hours confirm a positive pathergy reaction.
in_text_mentions: A pathergy test was performed to support the diagnosis (Figure 2A, 2B). The test showed multiple erythematous papular lesions (2-3 mm in diameter) with surrounding erythema at the needle puncture sites within 48 hours, corresponding to a 1+ to 2+ positive reaction as per standard grading criteria (Table 3). This positive pathergy response is diagnostically significant, reflecting the abnormal hyperreactive inflammatory response characteristic of Behçet’s disease and fulfilling one of the minor diagnostic criteria of the International Study Group (ISG) classification.

in_text_mentions: e patient returned to the operating room for emergent bioprosthetic valve removal and mechanical valve replacement. He was subsequently maintained on oral methylprednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, and warfarin. A year later, his clinical course was complicated by massive hemoptysis due to left lower lobar pulmonary artery aneurysm (Figure 15 A,B) rupture that required urgent left lower lobectomy. Since then, the patient required a prolonged hospitalization in the critical care unit for acute respiratory failure, hemorrhagic and septic shock but has been slowly making a good clinical recovery.

panels.rationale: Single-panel OCT macula map of the left eye from a patient with Behçet's disease. The in-text explicitly cites this figure in the context of retinal involvement characterized by periphlebitis and vascular sheathing suggestive of retinal vasculitis, and the article title is disease-focused, satisfying panel-specific attribution. The OCT displays retinal thickness distribution of the macula; attribution to Behçet's retinal vasculitis rests on the direct in-text reference to Figure 3. Confidence is moderate because the OCT shows retinal thickness rather than directly visualizing the retinal vascular changes (periphlebitis, vascular sheathing) of vasculitis.

in_text_mentions: nt on pinhole testing. Active inflammatory signs were present, including a faint anterior chamber flare and Grade II vitreous haze. Chronic complications were also observed, such as bilateral posterior subcapsular cataracts (PSCC+) and posterior synechiae (pupillary adhesions to the lens) in the left eye (Table 5). Retinal involvement was evident, characterized by periphlebitis and vascular sheathing, findings suggestive of retinal vasculitis (Figure 3). Collectively, these features reflected a severe, panocular inflammatory process necessitating urgent and intensive immunosuppressive therapy.

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: 'Multiple purpuric maculopapular lesions extending from both the lower legs to the dorsum of the feet'; in-text: 'multiple palpable purpuric maculopapular lesions on the bilateral lower legs, dorsum of the feet and hands' with biopsy-proven leukocytoclastic vasculitis in a patient with intestinal Behçet's disease (article title).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clear clinical photograph of palpable purpuric maculopapular lesions on the lower legs and feet. The disease-focused article title explicitly places these lesions in a patient with intestinal Behçet's disease, skin biopsy confirmed leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and the provided vocabulary includes leukocytoclastic vasculitis as a Behçet's disease finding, so attribution to behcet_disease is directly supported. Cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a recognized but less common Behçet's manifestation, hence variant typicality. B: Clear clinical photograph of hemorrhagic blisters and palpable purpura on the dorsum of the hand, the same biopsy-proven leukocytoclastic vasculitis lesion distribution described in the in-text mentions. The disease-focused article title ties these lesions to intestinal Behçet's disease, and the vocabulary lists leukocytoclastic vasculitis as a Behçet's finding, supporting behcet_disease attribution. in_text_mentions: ere followed 4-days later by purpura on his lower extremities. panels.body_site: external genitalia / vulva (vulvar and perineal region)
panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the female external genitalia showing multiple well-demarcated ulcerative lesions with purulent exudate, in an article whose title explicitly attributes genital ulceration to Behçet's disease. The appearance and caption are consistent with recurrent genital aphthous ulcers, a classic mucocutaneous manifestation of Behçet's disease. The in-text note that no active verrucous lesions were present elsewhere supports attribution to Behçet's genital ulceration rather than an STD or HPV-related lesion. Disease attribution is specific (Behçet's disease) via the article title plus a captioned manifestation; an arrow annotation is present but does not obscure the finding.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the vulvar region showing an ulcerative lesion on the left labium majus with erythema, induration, crusting, and scant mucopurulent exudate. Consent for publication was obtained, so no third-party restriction applies. No annotations are present.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial ADC map from a real patient in a Behçet's disease case report; the caption describes altered signal in the left basal ganglia extending to the left thalamus, midbrain and pons, matching the classic brainstem/diencephalic MRI pattern of parenchymal neuro-Behçet disease. The patient had recurrent oral and genital ulcers, supporting Behçet's attribution. [raw subtype: parenchymal_neurobehcet] B: Axial T2-weighted MRI from the same Behçet's disease patient showing the diencephalic/brainstem lesion with ventricular compression, a recognized parenchymal neuro-Behçet manifestation; disease attribution supported by the case-report title and the patient's recurrent oral and genital ulcers. [raw subtype: parenchymal_neurobehcet] C: Coronal T2-weighted MRI from the same Behçet's disease patient demonstrating the extent of the left basal ganglia/thalamus/midbrain/pons lesion; consistent with parenchymal neuro-Behçet disease as described in the...

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the back showing a widespread acneiform/follicular papulopustular eruption. The in-text explicitly lists 'folliculitis on the back' among the accepted Behçet disease criteria the patient met, and the vocabulary maps folliculitis-like pustules to the Behçet acneiform pustular eruption (synonyms include 'folliculitis-like pustules' and 'Behçet pustules'). Although the article title notes Trichophyton rubrum was cultured from these lesions, the eruption was clinically counted as a Behçet skin manifestation, so the panel is attributed to behcet_disease as a variant (recognized but less classic) skin presentation. No stated age or ethnicity; skin appears light-toned under warm lighting; no annotations present.

panels.figure_caption: folliculitis of the back
in_text_mentions: On physical examination, the patient had the accepted criteria of BD, painful sores in the mouth referred to as “aphthous ulcers,” genital ulcers, and folliculitis on the back (Figure 1).

The patient was initially managed with several courses of topical steroids to reduce the inflammation of the back. However, because of the lack of significant improvement, he was referred to our hospital for further investigation. Back lesions were noted to be sterile, resembled folliculitis, and had an acne-like appearance (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel H&E histopathology (×10) of tricuspid valve tissue from a Behçet's disease endocarditis case (article title: 'Frenemies within: An Endocarditis Case in Behçet's Disease'). The image shows neoformation vessels with subocclusive intimal hyperplasia (arrows) and siderophages, representing reparative vascular changes in the valve. The vascular pathology is attributed to Behçet's disease vasculitis. Cardiac involvement in Behçet's is uncommon, making this a variant presentation. No skin, ethnicity, or age information is available for this histology panel.
panels.attribution_text: Moroșan et al. Frenemies within: An Endocarditis Case in Behçet's Disease.. Journal of personalized medicine 2021. doi:10.3390/jpm11080728. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Tricuspid valve reparative changes; neoformation vessels with subocclusive intimal hyperplasia; siderophages after valve hemorrhage (Hematoxylin Eosin stain (HE) stain × 10).
in_text_mentions: entricle were found to be severely enlarged. The tricuspid valve was completely destructured and giant vegetations replaced the cusps. The valve histology showed a tricuspid valve with multiple reparative changes. Giant, multinucleate and foamy cells and siderophages after repeated hemorrhages were noted (Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 6 and Figure 7). Also, neoformation vessels with subocclusive intimal hyperplasia were found as well. A mural endocarditis was also present (Figure 5). Calcification and fibrosis involving the valve and the vegetation were observed (Figure 8 and Figure 9).

panels.rationale: Single-panel Gram-stained histology (40×) of tissue from a genital ulcer in a Behçet's disease patient, whose genital ulceration was being evaluated to exclude sexually transmitted infection (Treponema non-reactive; Figure 3). The genital ulcer is a recognized BD manifestation and the image is patient-derived, so it qualifies as a real patient image of a BD manifestation; the visibly present Gram-positive cocci are an incidental/infectious microscopic finding not specific to BD histology (no leukocytoclastic vasculitis is described), hence recorded in proposed_findings rather than a BD vocabulary key. The caption does not attribute the image to another disease, so disease_key is behcet_disease with no vocabulary-supported subtype. Skin tone is not assessable on microscopy; no age or ethnicity is stated; arrows annotate the organisms.
panels.attribution_text: Arkania et al. Behçet's Disease in a Patient With Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma: A Case of Genital Ulceration Resembling a Sexually Transmitted Disease.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.91050. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histological examination of genital ulcers with Gram staining showing the presence of Gram-positive cocci (40×).
in_text_mentions: For this patient, genital ulcers needed to be further evaluated to determine the underlying etiology. Several possible differential diagnoses that needed to be considered included BD, genital herpes, chancroid ulcers, and syphilis. On laboratory examination, the HIV examination showed non-reactive results (Table 1), while the Treponema examination showed negative results (Figure 3).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Real patient close-up of the nose with hemorrhagic vesicles/pustules and surrounding erythema, a mucocutaneous manifestation of Behçet's disease in this case; maps to the acneiform pustular eruption vocabulary item, but the hemorrhagic/necrotic quality makes it a less common (variant) form. B: Intraoral photograph of a hard palate erosion, i.e. recurrent oral aphthous-type ulceration, the cardinal mucosal manifestation of Behçet's disease in this case. Assessable surface is predominantly inflamed mucosa, so skin phototype is not assessable. The hard palate (keratinized) site is less typical for aphthae, hence variant rather than classic. C: Clinical photograph of both hands showing erosive lesions of varying ages with surrounding erythema, part of the hemorrhagic vesicle/bulla/erosion flare described in-text for this Behçet's disease case with trunk sparing. No exact vocabulary key exists for extremity erosions, so the clearly...

in_text_mentions: identified on the upper palate. The skin lesions then progressed within one week to hemorrhagic vesicles, bullae, and erosions with surrounding erythema involving the right ear, nose, eyebrows, distal extremities, and buttocks (Figure 1), with notable trunk sparing. The penile lesion evolved to necrotic ulceration within five days of onset, requiring surgical debridement during a prior hospitalization. The patient developed arthralgias during his hospitalization course and reported two distinct episodes of oral ulceration with nasal mucosal involvement, denying any ocular symptoms throughout.

panels.rationale: Single OCT 3D macula report (both eyes, OD and OS) from a Behçet's disease patient. The caption/in-text explicitly attribute the bilateral OCT findings to ocular involvement in Behçet's disease: disrupted retinal architecture, intraretinal fluid, bilateral macular thickness variations indicative of inflammatory edema, possible cystoid macular changes and RPE irregularities consistent with inflammatory retinopathy. Behçet's posterior-segment involvement is characteristically retinal vasculitis, so the closest vocabulary finding is behcet_disease_retinal_vasculitis; the directly visible OCT consequences (intraretinal fluid, cystoid macular edema, macular thickening, RPE irregularity) are added as proposed findings. Real patient ophthalmic image, no third-party restriction, adequately annotated (scan grid, ETDRS map, thickness values). Confidence tempered because the OCT visualizes the macular consequences of inflammatory retinopathy rather than retinal vessels/vitreous haze directly. [raw subtype: ocular]

in_text_mentions: Ocular examination revealed markedly reduced visual acuity in both eyes, accompanied by refractive error (Table 1). Fundoscopic evaluation demonstrated characteristic findings consistent with ocular involvement in Behçet’s disease (Figure 1).

Cross-sectional B-scans demonstrated retinal layer disruption, intraretinal inflammatory changes, possible cystoid macular changes, and surface irregularities consistent with inflammatory retinopathy. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) cross-sectional analysis in both eyes revealed disrupted retinal architecture, intraretinal fluid accumulation, and bilateral macular thickness variations indicative of inflammatory edema, along with irregularities of the retinal pigment (Figure 1).

in_text_mentions: We performed transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) that detected a 7×15 mm hyperechogenic mass located in the right ventricle, adjacent to the interventricular septum, and a right atrial echogenic mass of 14×18 mm consistent with thrombus (Figure 1). Besides, TTE exploring the inferior vena cava (IVC), revealed an intraluminal mass consistent with thrombus causing turbulence of flow on color Doppler (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: At this time, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated for possible tricuspid valve endocarditis. The empiric anti-tuberculosis treatment regimen was continued. Thereafter, a cardiac MRI was performed showing diffuse tricuspid valve thickening, multiple enhancing masses on the tricuspid valve leaflets, mass-like thickening at the level of the tricuspid annulus with projection into the right atrium, and diffusely enhancing focal area of right ventricular wall thickening. Initial CT of the thorax revealed bilateral pulmonary arterial thrombosis (Figure 2A-B).

panels.rationale: Single close-up clinical photograph of the anterior shin showing scattered erythematous to violaceous papules and pustules on an erythematous base, with the caption explicitly noting absence of vesiculation (arguing against herpes simplex) and absence of ulceration/necrosis. The symmetric maculopapular eruption with pustular evolution is a recognized Behçet's disease skin manifestation matching the vocabulary entry for a pustular acneiform eruption; the disease-focused article title pairs Behçet's disease with this captioned manifestation. The in-text describes the patient as an immunocompetent adult. Skin appears light and adequately lit. No arrows or labels are present. Confidence is moderate because the article ultimately attributes the eruption to Coxsackievirus mimicking Behçet's disease, but among the configured target diseases the lesion morphology best fits Behçet's pustular eruption rather than HSV.

in_text_mentions: On presentation, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Physical examination revealed irregular vulvar and perineal ulcerations with whitish discoloration and no purulent drainage, along with multiple shallow, round-to-oval oral ulcers with erythematous borders involving the buccal mucosa, ranging from approximately 3 to 5 mm in diameter. The lower-extremity lesions consisted of a symmetric maculopapular eruption with pustular evolution (Figures 1, 2). No lymphadenopathy was appreciated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient H&E (40X) of resected intestine in a Behct's disease case (article title); full-thickness chronic inflammatory infiltrate at the ulcer site with necrosis and granulation tissue and adjacent colonic-type mucosa ('Clear ulcer boundary'), i.e., intestinal Behct's ulceration. No vocabulary key exists for intestinal ulceration, so the visible finding is recorded in proposed_findings; vasculitis terminology is not propagated to this panel. [raw subtype: intestinal involvement] B: CD79a immunohistochemistry on the resected colonic specimen from the Behct's patient showing polyclonal proliferation of B lymphocytes differentiated from plasma cells, characterizing the ulcer-site chronic inflammatory infiltrate (reactive, excluding lymphoma). panels.figure_caption: Microscopic views of vasculitis-induced intestinal necrosis: (A) full-thickness infiltration by chronic inflammatory cells at ulcer site, with necrosis and granulation tissue formation (H&E, 40X); (B) polyclonal proliferation of B lymphocytes differentiated from plasma cells (CD79a, 40X); and (C) mural infiltration of vessels by inflammatory cells and visible thrombosis, with luminal narrowing or obliteration—note partial arterial wall disruption and prominent histiocytic aggregates inside venous channels at ulcer base (H&E, 200X).
in_text_mentions: Histologic sections of resected colon confirmed vasculitis-associated intestinal necrosis. Full-thickness chronic inflammatory cell infiltrates were evident at ulcerative sites, in addition to necrosis and granulation tissue formation. Some blood vessels showed inflammatory mural infiltrates and visible thromboses, with luminal narrowing or complete obliteration ( Figure 1 ).
